A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MG-Select research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the expanded supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and Franka robot experiments, including benchmark success rates, component ablations, and inference-latency measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds CALVIN evaluation, MiniVLA experiments, a RoboMonkey comparison, and further diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed sampling procedure, masked-reference KL scoring, token aggregation, joint-training objective, and single-prefill deployment remain unchanged. MiniVLA evaluation applies existing text-masking and aggregation choices; the additional explanations and experiments do not establish a revised MG-Select algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds CALVIN with training environments A/B/C and zero-shot testing in environment D, evaluating chains of up to five instructions across its manipulation tasks. This substantially extends coverage to another environment-transfer and sequential-instruction setting. RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and the original real-world tasks are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds an actual external-verifier comparison using a modified RoboMonkey on SIMPLER-WidowX (Table 14); v1 only discussed that method. It also adds vanilla MiniVLA versus MiniVLA with MG-Select on LIBERO (Table 13). The former introduces a central comparison category absent from v1's evaluated selection methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include CALVIN's ABC-to-D evaluation with 1,000 instructions and chain-completion metrics, MiniVLA training for 30k iterations with batch size 128, and a RoboMonkey comparison fixing sampling temperature to 0.1 and N=4 while removing perturbation and voting. Additional studies extend candidate counts to 64 and evaluate truncated-action reconstruction using normalized MAE. Existing Appendix A settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds dropout-ratio sensitivity, SIMPLER aggregation ablations, a model-scale study, LIBERO failure cases, candidate-KL diagnostics, and an action-reconstruction analysis supporting token truncation (Appendices D, G, H). Table 5 also expands candidate-count and aggregation-span sweeps. These investigate several previously untested design choices and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports means, medians, and interquartile ranges of KL scores across four candidate actions. This is descriptive statistical reporting, not benchmark confidence intervals. The existing three-seed success-rate averaging and five-seed latency protocol remain, with no stated increase in repeated runs or new significance testing.

E6.justification: Table 6 revises OpenVLA's average from 69.2 to 69.1 and its MG-Select counterpart from 70.8 to 71.7 without explaining the changes. New results include MiniVLA averages of 54.1 versus 60.5, CALVIN average chain lengths of 3.69 versus 3.86, and modified RoboMonkey versus MG-Select success rates of 50.7 versus 50.3. Numerous ablation, latency, and diagnostic findings are also added; the original RoboCasa, SIMPLER, and real-world headline scores remain.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a theorem and complete derivation establishing that masked-reference entropy increases with temperature, with derivative Var(z)/tau^3 >= 0. v1 supplied an empirical temperature rationale but no corresponding theorem or proof. This establishes the entropy property, not a guarantee of improved action selection.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the assertion that masking ensures maximum uncertainty to providing action uncertainty. The abstract replaces numerical highlights with a broader statement about reliable selection and benchmark improvements, while those numerical claims remain in the introduction. The principal verifier-free selection and joint-training contributions are retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains how unnecessary stochasticity can harm simple LIBERO tasks, proposes reasons for poor performance at low and high dropout ratios, and discusses domain-dependent aggregation spans. New KL visualizations and reconstruction analysis support interpretations of task-sensitive confidence and token truncation. It also explicitly weighs marginal gains beyond four candidates against computational cost.

D1.justification: v2 provides targeted implementation details for MiniVLA and CALVIN, specifies RoboMonkey's LLaVA-7B verifier and comparison modifications, and identifies the RTX A6000 used for that latency comparison. Table 10 newly identifies an A100 for existing latency measurements. The original training configurations and deployment search ranges remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to MiniVLA and CALVIN and develops its empirical positioning against the already-cited RoboMonkey. The main related-work discussion and distinction between intrinsic confidence and external verifiers are otherwise retained.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives limited abstract, conclusion, terminology, heading, and cross-reference edits, alongside an updated publication header and acknowledgments. New appendices organize the added material, and the unchanged LLM disclosure moves from Appendix D to I. Existing sections are not extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 11–15 and Figures 4–6, introducing additional comparison tables, failure rollouts, KL box plots, and a reconstruction-error scatter plot. Tables 5 and 10 gain rows. Figure 3 is relocated and redrawn with candidate counts through 64 and an expanded latency axis; Figures 1–2 are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct external-verifier comparison and substantive failure analysis despite their importance to its motivation. v2 addresses these gaps through Table 14 and Figure 4, while sensitivity studies, model-scale evaluation, and CALVIN results substantially strengthen the evidence and clarify applicability. The RoboMonkey comparison concerns a modified verifier-only procedure, and the revised OpenVLA scores remain unexplained. These limitations constrain particular conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in comparative support and diagnostic understanding.
